item.description: 5 Points Gallery is proud to present Durham Sweet Durham, a new exhibition of oil paintings by Featured Artist Jim McKeon celebrating the vibrant soul of the Bull City through crisp realism and touches of fantasy. From historic brick warehouses to the wild banks of the Eno River, familiar Durham landscapes become evocative scenes of memory, community, and place. Throughout the gallery, visitors can also enjoy work by our ten Triangle-based artists, offering a refreshing mix of painting, sculpture, fused glass, mixed media, and finely crafted furniture, with each artist bringing a distinct creative perspective. Join us for the Opening Reception on Friday, September 18, 2026, from 6–9 pm to meet the artist. Durham Sweet Durham runs from September 17 through October 10, 2026. item.title: Buena Vista Social Club — Fri Sep 25, 7:30 PM — DPAC Presented by First Horizon
item.description:
A Remarkable Blend of Music, Dance and Heart It’s been years since legendary singer Omara Portuondo last entered a recording studio. Once known as the “Queen of Feeling,” her voice was celebrated throughout Cuba – until she vanished from the spotlight. But when an ambitious young record producer brings her a rare opportunity, the elusive diva must finally reckon with her past. Hailed as a “jaw-dropping, soul-stirring must see” (The Washington Post), the Tony® and GRAMMY® Award-winning BUENA VISTA SOCIAL CLUB™ is a journey through music and memory into the beating heart of Havana. A world-class company brings the story of the iconic album to thrilling life in this tale of big dreams, second chances, and music that needs no translation.
Source: Downtown Durham Inc

item.title: The Midlife Replenish — Sat Sep 26, 3:00 PM — Yoga Off East
item.description:
A nourishing mini-retreat for women navigating the physical, emotional, and energetic shifts of midlife. This season of life is rarely linear, and neither is the experience of living in a changing body while balancing work, family, caregiving, and personal growth. Together, we’ll create space to slow down, reconnect, and replenish through gentle movement, breathwork, reflection, and meaningful connection. The retreat is designed to support nervous system regulation, ease tension, build strength, and foster a sense of grounding and renewal. Along the way, we’ll honor both the challenges and the wisdom that emerge during this chapter of life, making room for humor, community, and shared experience. All bodies, backgrounds, and stages are welcome. Come exactly as you are: tired, strong, overwhelmed, hopeful, curious, or somewhere in between. Leave feeling supported, restored, and more connected to yourself and others.
Source: Downtown Durham Inc

item.title: J Weeks Entertainment Presents "Getting Married Again" Stage Play — Sat Sep 26, 5:00 PM — Durham Arts Council
item.description:
Getting Married Again is a hilarious and heartfelt new stage play that explores the complicated road of family, forgiveness, and second chances. Blending laugh-out-loud comedy with raw emotional drama, the production follows a man determined to rebuild the family he lost while confronting the past he tried to outrun. This powerful story highlights the preservation of family, the courage to rise again, and the truth that love, no matter how messy, is worth fighting for. Opening Night on Saturday, September 26, will feature the return of the Black Tie Affair and Art Show, beginning at 5:30 PM. Guests will enjoy a red carpet experience and an exclusive exhibition of original paintings, drawings, and sculptures created by talented local artists before the curtain rises at 7:00 PM. The evening continues J Weeks Entertainment’s commitment to creating a space where local visual artists and live theater can thrive together.
Source: Downtown Durham Inc

item.title: Return of the Wild: A Lewis and Clark Wildlife Resurvey — Thu Oct 8, 7:00 PM — Downtown Raleigh
item.description: Two hundred and twenty years after Lewis and Clark documented the animals of the west in their journals, we retraced their route with camera traps to find out what we lost, what’s still there, and what it took to save America’s wildlife. Dr. Roland Kays, head of the Biodiversity Research Lab at NCMNS and professor at NC State University, will share the story of his team’s expedition across the United States in this special lecture event. Doors open at 6:30PM. The lecture begins in the WRAL 3D Theater at 7PM. This event is free and open to the public. Two men writing down every animal they encountered, most of which they’d never seen before. item.title: Historical Hearth Cooks Demonstration — Sat Oct 10, 12:00 PM — President James K. Polk Historic Site
item.description:
​Beverages during the late 18th and early 19th century generally consisted of some form of alcohol, even for the children. Fresh water could be hazardous to drink and with no refrigeration, alcoholic beverages were often consumed. One of these drinks, a “small beer” could be made at home and drank by the family. The ingredients were simple, barley malt, hops and water. It could be cooked over the daily fire and though it didn’t have along shelf life, it was easy enough to make in big or small batches. Today we will go through the process of making a small beer and also serve a Ranquiem of cheese.
“The New and Easy method of Cookery” by Elizabeth Cleland “Seeking the historical cook” by Kay Mos
Source: NC Cultural Resources

item.description: This North Carolina State Natural Area is a gem, with a diversity of natural plant and animal communities not found anywhere else in the Triangle region. Join Paul Manos, Duke biology professor and Duke Herbarium curator, and Alec Motten, professor emeritus, Duke University Department of Biology, on a two- to three-mile mountain hike of moderate difficulty. Both Alec and Paul bring a deep expertise in plants and ecology; they will “read” the landscape and give you a unique view of Occoneechee Mountain. Did you know that our modern Thanksgiving holiday largely has its origins in 1863? During the midst of the Civil War, President Lincoln proclaimed a day of Thanksgiving on the last Thursday of November to help heal the wounds of the nation and to restore peace and union.
Lincoln ultimately decided to make this Thanksgiving proclamation at the petition of Sarah Josepha Hale, editor of Godey's Lady's Book, who had advocated for such a holiday for over 15 years! This started an annual tradition which has been celebrated nationwide ever since.
For Lincoln and the loyal states in 1863, this Thanksgiving holiday allowed Americans to give thanks for major campaign victories (like Gettysburg) that year, for continued union of the loyal states, and blessings upon those who had lost loved ones in the war.

item.title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians — Wed Dec 23 — Presbyterian Heritage Center
item.description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority, and is published that it may go down to posterity.”
The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.
But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting.

Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. item.title: Applied Thematic Analysis (online) — Fri Sep 25, 10:00 AM
item.description:
It’s Monday morning and you open your qualitative research project folder. Thousands of pages of text, distributed across 90 in-depth interviews, await. What’s next? This workshop provides a roadmap for conducting an applied thematic analysis, through all major steps in the analytic process. Participants will learn the benefits of writing a qualitative data analysis plan, to ensure that the data collected are analyzed in a way that best informs the research question(s) and fulfills the study’s objectives.
The instructors will demonstrate how to inductively identify themes, transform those themes into codes, and aggregate codes into an evidence-based codebook that is easy to use and that will inform the study’s research question(s). Some time will be spent on the topic of integrating codes and interpreting thematic structure. Basic data reduction techniques will also be presented Hands-on exercises are included for those who wish to practice the concepts learned.

item.title: Dr. Dave Fossum | UNC Music Research Forum — Fri Sep 25, 3:30 PM — Person Hall
item.description: Dr. Dave Fossum, Arizona State University, National Humanities Center “What’s an Arrangement Worth?: Copyright, Folk Music, and the Value of Creativity in Turkey” Copyright is supposed to reward creators for their creativity. Yet there are no clear criteria for measuring the value of this creativity or how creative a work is. Drawing on a case study from my book, Copyright Consciousness, this talk links implicit criteria of creative value to a larger history of nation-building. The launching point for my inquiry is a policy of Turkey’s copyright collecting societies, who long offered arrangers of public domain folk music only a (10%) royalty on their arrangements (whereas a 100% royalty is common in most jurisdictions). While some arrangers complained about this policy, my ethnographic data reveal that many musicians found it natural.
